title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰莫我知也夫子貢曰何爲其莫知子
也子曰不怨天不尤人下學而上達知
我者其天乎
吳鋌
同考試官訓導倫　批　此題塲中類不得夫子發嘆意
是作獨中肯綮而詞理精到足式多士
考試官教諭孫　批　清脱古雅宜錄
考試官教授黃　批　精邃簡健
===
聖人之所以莫知者惟其不求人知也夫不求
人知聖學也此人之所以莫知而惟天知之也
與且春秋之世急人知者矜異行務實學者鮮
知名故人莫巳知固夫子所不患而所以莫知
者有未明焉乃其所深慮也于是有莫知之嘆
而子貢曰何爲其莫知焉其亦未知夫子之深
也從而語之曰道本通於天人學惟脩其在我
天有不得吾脩之未能也不敢怨也人有不合
punctuated:
第壹場

四書

「子曰：『莫我知也夫！』子貢曰：『何爲其莫知子也？』子曰：『不怨天，不尤人，下學而上達，知我者其天乎！』」

吳鋌

同考試官訓導倫批：此題塲中類不得夫子發嘆意，是作獨中肯綮，而詞理精到，足式多士。
考試官教諭孫批：清脱古雅，宜錄。
考試官教授黃批：精邃簡健。

聖人之所以莫知者，惟其不求人知也。夫不求人知，聖學也；此人之所以莫知，而惟天知之也與！且春秋之世，急人知者矜異行，務實學者鮮知名。故人莫巳知，固夫子所不患，而所以莫知者有未明焉，乃其所深慮也。于是有「莫知」之嘆。而子貢曰：「何爲其莫知焉？」其亦未知夫子之深也。從而語之曰：道本通於天人，學惟脩其在我。天有不得，吾脩之未能也，不敢怨也；人有不合，
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said, "Alas, there is no one who knows me!" Zigong said, "Why is it that no one knows you?" The Master said, "I do not resent Heaven, nor do I blame men. Learning from what is below and penetrating what is above—is it not Heaven that knows me?"

Wu Ting 吳鋌

Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Lun 倫, comments: On this topic, the candidates in the examination hall generally failed to grasp the Master's intention in uttering this sigh. This composition alone hits the crucial point, and its diction and reasoning are refined and thorough, sufficient to serve as a model for the many scholars.
Examiner, Instructor Sun 孫, comments: Clear, unencumbered, clásico, and elegant; it ought to be selected for inclusion.
Examiner, Professor Huang 黃, comments: Refined, profound, concise, and vigorous.

The reason the sage is known by no one is simply that he does not seek to be known by others. Now, not seeking to be known by others is sagely learning; is this not why other men do not know him, and why Heaven alone knows him! Moreover, in the age of the Spring and Autumn period, those eager to be known by others boasted of eccentric conduct, while those who devoted themselves to substantive learning rarely achieved a известных reputation. Therefore, that others did not know him was certainly not something the Master worried about; rather, that the reason why no one knew him remained unclear—this was what deeply concerned him. Thereupon he uttered the sigh that "no one knows me." Yet when Zigong asked, "Why is it that no one knows you?", he too did not yet understand the Master deeply. Accordingly, the Master spoke to him, saying: The Way inherently connects Heaven and humanity, and learning consists solely in cultivating what lies within oneself. If something is not obtained from Heaven, it is because my self-cultivation is not yet adequate; I dare not resent it. If there is a lack of harmony with other men, …

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
吾脩之未能也不敢尤也吾惟於天所賦予而
人所同得者爲之不厭恒亹亹以盡下學之功
而積之旣深自駸駸乎有上達之妙自志學而
從心循其序焉而已無異學也由知好而能樂
進以漸焉而已非强達也爲之自我者如是而
欲人之知我也無繇矣意者惟天無心惟理可
契庶其知我而未可必也天或我知不爲徒學
人卽莫知而可無憾也賜也其謂之何要之惟
夫子之道達諸天故人莫能知惟人莫能知乃
===
所以爲夫子然則人之知不知又何足言也雖
然夫子豈誠無意於人之知不知哉不見知而
不悔者歸之聖莫巳知而斯巳者謂之果其樂
天憂世之心可想也道大莫容人莫予宗矣使
不以天之可信者自任天下萬世之學術將奚
賴焉是則夫子衛道之意也
道不遠人人之爲道而遠人不可以爲道
錢　溥
同考試官教諭譚　批體認不遠人處與切關鎖更覺
punctuated:
吾脩之未能也，不敢尤也。吾惟於天所賦予而人所同得者，爲之不厭，恒亹亹以盡下學之功；而積之旣深，自駸駸乎有上達之妙。自志學而從心，循其序焉而已，無異學也；由知好而能樂，進以漸焉而已，非强達也。爲之自我者如是，而欲人之知我也無繇矣。意者惟天無心，惟理可契，庶其知我，而未可必也。天或我知，不爲徒學；人卽莫知，而可無憾也。賜也其謂之何？」要之，惟夫子之道達諸天，故人莫能知；惟人莫能知，乃所以爲夫子。然則人之知不知，又何足言也！雖然，夫子豈誠無意於人之知不知哉？不見知而不悔者歸之聖，莫巳知而斯巳者謂之果，其樂天憂世之心可想也。道大莫容，人莫予宗矣，使不以天之可信者自任，天下萬世之學術將奚賴焉？是則夫子衛道之意也。

道不遠人，人之爲道而遠人，不可以爲道。
錢　溥
同考試官教諭譚　批：體認不遠人處與切，關鎖更覺
translation_en:
… is because my self-cultivation is not yet sufficient; I dare not blame them. Only in that which Heaven has endowed and which all men share in common do I work without tiring, constantly and tirelessly exhausting the effort of studying what is below; and when this accumulation becomes deep, I naturally and gradually attain the subtlety of penetrating what is above. From setting my heart on learning to following my heart's desire, I simply follow the proper sequence, without any aberrant learning; from knowing and loving the Way to delighting in it, I simply advance gradually, without forcing my way to penetration. Since what I do from within myself is like this, there is no way I could seek for others to know me. Perhaps only Heaven, which has no ulterior mind and can be tallied with solely through principle, might know me—though even that cannot be taken for granted. If Heaven perhaps knows me, then I have not studied in vain; even if no man knows me, I can be without regret. Si [Zigong], what do you say to this?"

In sum, it is precisely because the Master's Way penetrated to Heaven that no one could know him, and it is precisely because no one could know him that he was the Master. If so, whether others knew him or not is hardly worth mentioning! Even so, was the Master truly indifferent to whether others knew him or not? One who is not known and feels no regret he attributed to the sage, while one who gives up as soon as no one knows him he called resolute [in a narrow sense]; from this, his heart that delighted in Heaven yet worried for the world can be imagined. His Way was so great that the world could not accommodate it, and no one took him as their master; had he not taken upon himself that in which Heaven could be trusted, on what would the scholarship of the empire for ten thousand generations rely? This, then, was the Master's intention in defending the Way.

"The Way is not far from man; when men practice the Way and distance themselves from man, it cannot be considered the Way."
Qian Pu 錢溥
Associate Examiner and Instructor Tan 譚 comments: His personal realization of the point that "the Way is not far from man" is fitting and incisive [?], and the structural transitions feel even more…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
精神非見道者不能到
考試官教諭孫　批　精詣不落言詮
考試官教授黃　批　理明詞古
中庸論道本在人而爲道者失之遠也夫道即
人之所以爲人者也曾謂遠人以爲之而可爲
道哉夫子意曰道體無爲待人而爲則爲道固
吾人之責也世有遠人以爲道者豈以道誠遠
人乎哉吾謂道原於天是道即天之所以生人
者也有人斯有道矣道率乎性是道即人之所
以成性者也性在則道在矣天下無人外之道
又豈有遠人之道哉人之爲道者亦惟不遠人
以爲之而道即在是矣夫苟以道爲至大也人
不足以盡之也而馳神於玄遠之歸爲道至難
===
也非人可幾及也而役志於難爲之事生人之
理爲道而乃求之人理之外焉迹其所爲若足
以高天下而外人不可以言道也曷可爲道哉
率性之懿爲道而乃索之人性所無焉雖其所
爲或足以述后世而遠人即所以遠道也道曷
punctuated:
精神，非見道者不能到。
考試官教諭孫批：精詣不落言詮。
考試官教授黃批：理明詞古。

《中庸》論道本在人，而爲道者失之遠也。夫道即人之所以爲人者也，曾謂遠人以爲之，而可爲道哉？夫子意曰：道體無爲，待人而爲，則爲道固吾人之責也。世有遠人以爲道者，豈以道誠遠人乎哉？吾謂道原於天，是道即天之所以生人者也，有人斯有道矣；道率乎性，是道即人之所以成性者也，性在則道在矣。天下無人外之道，又豈有遠人之道哉？人之爲道者，亦惟不遠人以爲之，而道即在是矣。夫苟以道爲至大也，人不足以盡之也，而馳神於玄遠之歸；爲道至難也，非人可幾及也，而役志於難爲之事。生人之理爲道，而乃求之人理之外焉，迹其所爲，若足以高天下，而外人不可以言道也，曷可爲道哉？率性之懿爲道，而乃索之人性所無焉，雖其所爲，或足以述后世，而遠人即所以遠道也，道曷
translation_en:
…spirited; one who has not perceived the Way could not attain this.
Examiner and Confucian Instructor (jiaoyu) Sun comments: Profoundly accomplished, without falling into the trap of mere verbal explanation.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies (jiaoshou) Huang comments: The principles are clear and the diction is archaic in style.

The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) discusses how the Way inherently resides in man, yet those who practice the Way err by placing it at a distance. Now, the Way is simply that by which humans are human; how could one say that practicing it while distancing oneself from human beings can be considered practicing the Way? The Master's meaning is this: The substance of the Way does not act of itself, but awaits human beings in order to be practiced; thus, practicing the Way is inherently our responsibility as humans. When there are those in the world who distance themselves from humanity to practice the Way, is it because they think the Way truly is distant from man? I say that the Way originates from Heaven, which means the Way is that by which Heaven gives birth to humans; where there are humans, there is the Way. The Way follows our nature, which means the Way is that by which humans complete their nature; where human nature exists, the Way exists. Under Heaven there is no Way outside of humanity, so how could there be a Way that is distant from man? Those who practice the Way need only practice it without distancing themselves from humanity, and the Way is right there. Now, suppose someone regards the Way as supremely great—something that humans are insufficient to exhaust—and thus lets his spirit gallop toward abstruse and distant ends; or regards the Way as supremely difficult—something that humans can scarcely hope to reach—and thus enslaves his will to undertakings that are difficult to perform. The principle of human life is the Way, yet he seeks it outside the principles of humanity; if we trace what he does, it may seem lofty enough to tower over the world, yet once one excludes humanity one cannot speak of the Way—how can that be considered practicing the Way? The admirable goodness of following human nature is the Way, yet he searches for it in what human nature does not possess; even if what he does might suffice to be recounted to later generations, to distance oneself from humanity is ipso facto to distance oneself from the Way—how can the Way…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
可爲哉是道惟不遠人以爲之則雖位天地育
萬物而道無不可爲何也凡吾人分内事皆道
也遠人以爲之則雖超天地離萬物而道終不
可爲何也凡非吾人所能爲皆非道也爲道者
其審諸抑論道本至虛體道貴實實者人之謂
也故子臣弟友人也庸德庸言所以踐其實也
夫子之體道亦不過如是彼鑿虛而高遠其說
者是欲賢於夫子也其去道也不益遠乎
君子之守脩其身而天下平
===
邵元亨
同考試官訓導孫　批　講脩身處不著工夫發明守約施博最爲得旨塗養士也錄之
考試官教諭孫　批　淵然之識蒼然之語
考試官教授黃　批　雄邁不羣
君子惟本諸身以成治道之所以善也夫道曰
脩身至約也而平天下不外是焉兹其所以爲
善道與且道惟守約而施博者爲善道則凡執
之寡要而其用易窮者未善也不有平天下之
punctuated:
可爲哉？是道惟不遠人以爲之，則雖位天地、育萬物，而道無不可爲。何也？凡吾人分内事，皆道也。遠人以爲之，則雖超天地、離萬物，而道終不可爲。何也？凡非吾人所能爲，皆非道也。爲道者，其審諸！抑論道本至虛，體道貴實。實者，人之謂也。故子、臣、弟、友，人也；庸德、庸言，所以踐其實也。夫子之體道，亦不過如是。彼鑿虛而高遠其說者，是欲賢於夫子也，其去道也不益遠乎！

君子之守，脩其身而天下平。
邵元亨
同考試官訓導孫批：講脩身處不著工夫，發明守約施博最爲得旨。塗養士也，錄之。
考試官教諭孫批：淵然之識，蒼然之語。
考試官教授黃批：雄邁不羣。

君子惟本諸身以成治，道之所以善也。夫道曰脩身，至約也；而平天下不外是焉，兹其所以爲善道與！且道惟守約而施博者爲善道，則凡執之寡要而其用易窮者，未善也。不有平天下之
translation_en:
… can the Way be practiced? Therefore, if one practices the Way without distancing it from humanity, then even to establish Heaven and Earth in their proper places and nurture the myriad things—nothing in the Way is impracticable. Why is this? Because everything that lies within our human duty is the Way. If one practices it by distancing it from humanity, then even if one transcends Heaven and Earth and detaches from the myriad things, the Way ultimately cannot be practiced. Why is this? Because anything beyond what we as human beings are able to do is not the Way. Let those who practice the Way examine this carefully! Moreover, in discussing the Way, its essence is supremely intangible, yet embodying the Way values substance. "Substance" refers to humanity. Therefore, son, minister, younger brother, and friend are human roles; ordinary virtues and ordinary words are the means to fulfill their substance. The Master's embodiment of the Way was nothing more than this. Those who bore into emptiness and make their doctrines lofty and remote wish to be worthier than the Master—are they not departing even further from the Way!

"What the gentleman holds fast to is cultivating his person, and thereby the world is brought to peace."
Shao Yuanheng 邵元亨
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Sun comments: Where it discusses cultivating the person, it does not belabor the effort required, and in elucidating how holding to the essential extends broadly in application, it grasps the main purport best. He is a scholar of well-grounded cultivation [?]; record it for publication.
Examiner and Instructor Sun comments: Profound insight and seasoned phrasing.
Examiner and Professor Huang comments: Vigorous, lofty, and extraordinary.

The gentleman simply roots his governance in his own person to bring order to completion; this is why the Way is good. Now, when the Way is spoken of as cultivating the person, it is most essential and concise; yet bringing peace to the world does not lie outside of this—is this not why it is a good Way? Furthermore, since only the Way that holds to the essential while extending broadly in application is the good Way, any approach that grasps little of what is essential and whose efficacy is easily exhausted is not yet good. Is there not the [gentleman] who brings peace to the world…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
君子乎蓋自吾身與天下言之吾身其約也實
天下所統會也天下其博也皆吾身所聯屬也
君子惟守欲其約焉故不以天下治天下也嘗
先天下以脩吾之身亦不以天下役吾身也惟
脩吾身以通之於天下以身作則而均平四海
有餘裕焉本端而末治何事規畫之煩也一人
建極而輯寧萬邦可坐致焉道立而化行何有
運量之勞也養之端莊靜一之中出之道濟天
下而無外是謂握其機要而神理備矣其篤恭
===
而天下平乎斂之幾微宥密之地推之曲成萬
物而不遺是謂不下堂序而王道達矣其垂拱
而天下治乎夫守止於身守何約也而天下平
焉施則博矣惟約也故其施爲不窮惟博也故
其守爲知要此所以爲君子之善道也抑是道
也語平天下若易易矣而身之脩也可易言哉
容止端矣而斯須不莊防檢密矣而一念少間
皆未可言脩也故孔子曰脩己以安百姓而必
本之敬焉是敬又脩身之約也否則施仁義而
punctuated: 君子乎？蓋自吾身與天下言之，吾身其約也，實天下所統會也；天下其博也，皆吾身所聯屬也。君子惟守欲其約焉，故不以天下治天下也，嘗先天下以脩吾之身；亦不以天下役吾身也，惟脩吾身以通之於天下。以身作則，而均平四海有餘裕焉。本端而末治，何事規畫之煩也？一人建極，而輯寧萬邦可坐致焉。道立而化行，何有運量之勞也？養之端莊靜一之中，出之道濟天下而無外，是謂握其機要而神理備矣，其「篤恭而天下平」乎！斂之幾微宥密之地，推之曲成萬物而不遺，是謂不下堂序而王道達矣，其「垂拱而天下治」乎！夫守止於身，守何約也，而天下平焉，施則博矣。惟約也，故其施爲不窮；惟博也，故其守爲知要。此所以爲君子之善道也。抑是道也，語平天下若易易矣，而身之脩也可易言哉？容止端矣，而斯須不莊；防檢密矣，而一念少間，皆未可言脩也。故孔子曰「脩己以安百姓」，而必本之敬焉。是敬又脩身之約也。否則施仁義而
translation_en: … superior man? For speaking in terms of one's own person and the Empire: one's own person is what is concise, yet it is truly the hub where the Empire converges; the Empire is what is broad, yet all of it is linked together by one's own person. Because the superior man desires that what he guards be concise, he does not use the Empire to govern the Empire, but always puts the cultivation of his own person ahead of the Empire; nor does he allow the Empire to enslave his own person, but simply cultivates his own person so as to extend it throughout the Empire. By making his person the standard, he brings equitable order to the Four Seas with ample ease to spare. When the root is upright and the branches are ordered, what need is there for the trouble of elaborate planning? When the One Man establishes the supreme standard, bringing harmony and peace to the myriad states can be achieved while sitting still. When the Way is established and transformation proceeds, what toil of management and calculation could there be? Nurturing it within solemnity, tranquility, and unity, and bringing it forth as the Way that aids the entire Empire without exclusion—this is called grasping the pivotal essentials so that marvelous principle is complete. Is this not "being devoutly reverent, and the Empire is brought to peace"? Concentrating it in the subtle, deep, and silent recesses, and extending it to bring all myriad things to their intricate fulfillment without omission—this is called not descending from the hall and yet causing the Kingly Way to reach everywhere. Is this not "letting the robes hang down with folded hands, and the Empire is governed"? Now, when what one guards stops at one's own person, how concise that guarding is! Yet when the Empire is brought to peace thereby, the application is broad indeed. Because it is concise, its application is inexhaustible; because its application is broad, what it guards is known to be the essential. This is why it is the good Way of the superior man. Yet as for this Way, speaking of bringing peace to the Empire seems easy enough, but can the cultivation of the person be spoken of lightly? Though one's deportment be upright, if for a single moment one is not solemn; though one's self-restraint be strict, if for a single thought there is the slightest lapse—none of this can yet be called cultivation. Therefore Confucius said, "Cultivate oneself so as to give peace to the hundred surnames," and he必ず rooted it in reverence. Thus reverence is in turn the concise essential of personal cultivation. Otherwise, even if one dispenses benevolence and righteousness and…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
慕唐虞卽脩身亦務摶儞何足以語道
易
含弘光大品物咸亨
吴鋌
同考試官訓導倫　批　發厚德亨物明徹簡淨深於易
者也取之
考試官教諭孫　批　詞約而意盡
考試官教授黃　批　典雅可式
象傳極賛坤德之厚因著物所由通也蓋含弘
===
光大坤德厚矣而品物之亨以之不可以識亨
之義乎象傳之意若曰坤之爲道配天者其體
也通物者其化也欲觀坤德之厚盍於是徵之
乎彼化機不能以遽顯必有藴之而爲含者含
矣弗弘德未厚也坤則藏生意於微茫而合萬
有以竝蓄蓋極天所覆皆坤之載也皆其所包
括也何如其含弘耶化機不容以終藏必有發
之而爲光者光矣弗大德未厚也坤則彰化工
於有象而煥生息於無窮蓋極地所載皆坤之
punctuated:
慕唐虞，卽脩身亦務摶儞，何足以語道？

《易》
「含弘光大，品物咸亨。」
吴鋌
同考試官訓導倫　批：發厚德亨物，明徹簡淨，深於《易》者也。取之。
考試官教諭孫　批：詞約而意盡。
考試官教授黃　批：典雅可式。

《象傳》極賛坤德之厚，因著物所由通也。蓋含弘光大，坤德厚矣，而品物之亨以之，不可以識亨之義乎？《象傳》之意若曰：坤之爲道，配天者其體也，通物者其化也。欲觀坤德之厚，盍於是徵之乎？彼化機不能以遽顯，必有藴之而爲含者；含矣弗弘，德未厚也。坤則藏生意於微茫，而合萬有以竝蓄。蓋極天所覆，皆坤之載也，皆其所包括也。何如其含弘耶！化機不容以終藏，必有發之而爲光者；光矣弗大，德未厚也。坤則彰化工於有象，而煥生息於無窮。蓋極地所載，皆坤之
translation_en:
…admire Tang and Yu, then even in cultivating the self one is merely pursuing breadth [?]; how could that suffice to speak of the Way?

Classic of Changes (Yi)
"Containing and vast, glorious and great, all things in their categories attain full development."
Wu Ting
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Lun, comments: He elucidates how capacious virtue brings things to full development in a manner that is clear, penetrating, concise, and pure—one who is profound in the Classic of Changes. Selected.
Examiner, Instructor Sun, comments: The words are economical, yet the meaning is exhausted.
Examiner, Professor Huang, comments: Refined and classical, worthy of serving as a model.

The "Commentary on the Judgments" (Tuanzhuan) praises to the utmost the capaciousness of the virtue of the Receptive (Kun), and thereby makes manifest that whereby all things achieve thorough development. Indeed, being containing and vast, glorious and great, the virtue of the Receptive is capacious indeed; and since the full development of the myriad categories of things depends upon this, can one not thereby recognize the meaning of "full development" (heng)?

The purport of the "Commentary on the Judgments" is as if to say: As for the Way of the Receptive, matching Heaven is its substance, and bringing things to thorough development is its transformative operation. If one wishes to observe the capaciousness of the virtue of the Receptive, why not verify it in this? That mechanism of transformation cannot suddenly become manifest; there must be that which stores it up so as to "contain" it. Yet if it contains without being "vast," its virtue is not yet capacious. The Receptive, however, conceals the impulse of life within the subtle and indistinct, and brings together the myriad existents to nourish them all side by side. Indeed, to the furthest limits of what Heaven covers, all is borne up by the Receptive, and all is encompassed by it. How containing and vast it is!

The mechanism of transformation cannot remain forever concealed; there must be that which puts it forth so as to be "glorious." Yet if it is glorious without being "great," its virtue is not yet capacious. The Receptive, however, displays the work of transformation in visible forms, and makes the growth and flourishing shine forth without end. Indeed, to the furthest limits of what Earth bears up, all is the Receptive's…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
含也皆其所發舒也何如其光大耶此誠坤之
合德於無疆者而物因以通矣機緘旣露而爲
形爲色皆欣欣以向榮朕兆已萌而成大成小
咸熙熙以竝育向方資元之理以爲性也此則
生理敷布而品物之各一其性者燦然條達焉
盛復有鬱而未舒者乎向方資元之氣以爲形
也此則氣機旁達而品物之各一其形者煥然
暢茂焉盛復有蓄而未通者乎夫由品物之亨
益以見坤德之厚由坤德之厚乃足配無疆之
===
乾矣而坤亨之義不從可知歟然德合無疆者
坤也應地無疆者君子也體易者誠能法坤之
厚德以載物使萬國咸盛之化與品物之咸亨
同一忻榮焉則所以賛化育而叅天地者又在
我矣
鼓之以雷霆潤之以風雨日月運行一寒
一暑　　孫思繼
同考試官訓導倫　批　題本平正最難裁制恭而是作結
punctuated:
含也，皆其所發舒也，何如其光大耶！此誠坤之合德於無疆者，而物因以通矣。機緘旣露，而爲形爲色，皆欣欣以向榮；朕兆已萌，而成大成小，咸熙熙以竝育。向方資元之理以爲性也，此則生理敷布，而品物之各一其性者，燦然條達焉，盛復有鬱而未舒者乎？向方資元之氣以爲形也，此則氣機旁達，而品物之各一其形者，煥然暢茂焉，盛復有蓄而未通者乎？夫由品物之亨，益以見坤德之厚；由坤德之厚，乃足配無疆之乾矣，而坤亨之義不從可知歟？然德合無疆者，坤也；應地無疆者，君子也。體易者誠能法坤之厚德以載物，使萬國咸盛之化，與品物之咸亨同一忻榮焉，則所以賛化育而叅天地者，又在我矣。

「鼓之以雷霆，潤之以風雨，日月運行，一寒一暑。」　　孫思繼
同考試官訓導倫　批：題本平正，最難裁制，恭而是作結
translation_en:
… holds is all that it unfolds and expands! How radiant and great it is! This truly is how Kun matches the boundless virtue [of Qian], and through it all things flourish and thrive. Once the hidden mechanism is revealed, taking on form and color, all things joyously grow toward splendor; once the subtle signs have sprouted, becoming great or small, all things harmoniously develop together. Previously, they were just drawing upon the principle of the primal origin to form their natures; now, the principle of life is spread forth, and the myriad things, each with its own distinct nature, develop in brilliant order—how could there still be [reading 盛 as 豈] anything pent up and unexpanded? Previously, they were just drawing upon the vital force of the primal origin to form their physical shapes; now, the vital mechanism reaches everywhere, and the myriad things, each with its own distinct form, flourish in vibrant abundance—how could there still be [reading 盛 as 豈] anything held back and unobstructed? Thus, from the flourishing of the myriad things, one sees even more clearly the thickness of Kun's virtue; and because of the thickness of Kun's virtue, it is worthy to match the boundless Qian. Can the meaning of Kun's flourishing not be understood from this? Yet that whose virtue matches the boundless is Kun; he who corresponds to the boundless earth is the noble man. If one who embodies the Changes can truly model himself on Kun's thick virtue in order to sustain all things—causing the transformative influence by which the myriad states all flourish [or: are all at peace, reading 盛 for 寧] to share in the same joyous splendor as the flourishing of the myriad things—then the means to assist the transforming and nourishing powers and to form a triad with Heaven and Earth will also rest with us.

"Rousing them with thunder and lightning, moistening them with wind and rain; the sun and moon move in their courses, now cold, now hot."
By Sun Siji 孫思繼.

Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor (xundao) Lun 倫 comments: The topic itself is plain and straightforward, making it most difficult to tailor and structure. [?] Yet this composition's structure…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
精當明易象昭然殆不凡之士
考試官教諭孫　批　確實不浮
考試官教授黃　批　明暢
觀象於天一易理之著見也蓋易以道陰陽也
則夫成象於天者孰非易理之著見哉且天一
陰陽也陰陽一變化也剛柔摩盪變化在易矣
即是以仰觀於天而其理不可見乎彼天之成
象一也自其搏擊而為雷霆焉和暢而為風雨
焉或鼓元氣而神其奮迅之能或潤萬物而普
===
其舒和之澤是其所以振化機而蘇羣動者若
是不同矣然雷霆者陰陽之義氣也風雨者陰
陽之仁氣也若有物焉以宰之而特不得其眹
者何莫非易理有以鼓潤之乎自其著明而為
日月焉變通而為寒暑焉或麗天普照而消息
盈虛之有常或隨時錯行而往來推遷之不紊
是其所以繼離照而成歲功者若是不一矣然
日月者陰陽之互藏其精也寒暑者陰陽之順
布其序也若有機焉以運之而特不得其端者
punctuated:
精當，明易象昭然，殆不凡之士。
考試官教諭孫批：確實不浮。
考試官教授黃批：明暢。

觀象於天，一易理之著見也。蓋易以道陰陽也，則夫成象於天者，孰非易理之著見哉？且天一陰陽也，陰陽一變化也。剛柔摩盪，變化在易矣；即是以仰觀於天，而其理不可見乎？彼天之成象一也：自其搏擊而為雷霆焉，和暢而為風雨焉，或鼓元氣而神其奮迅之能，或潤萬物而普其舒和之澤，是其所以振化機而蘇羣動者，若是不同矣；然雷霆者，陰陽之義氣也，風雨者，陰陽之仁氣也，若有物焉以宰之，而特不得其眹者，何莫非易理有以鼓潤之乎？自其著明而為日月焉，變通而為寒暑焉，或麗天普照而消息盈虛之有常，或隨時錯行而往來推遷之不紊，是其所以繼離照而成歲功者，若是不一矣；然日月者，陰陽之互藏其精也，寒暑者，陰陽之順布其序也，若有機焉以運之，而特不得其端者，
translation_en:
… precise and fitting, clearly illuminating the images of the Changes (Yi)—truly an extraordinary scholar.
Examiner and Instructor Sun [Sun Siji 孫思繼] comments: Solid and reliable, without superficiality.
Examiner and Professor Huang comments: Clear and fluent.

Observing the phenomena in the heavens, all are the manifest revelation of the principle of the Changes. For the Changes speaks of yin and yang; among those things that form images in the heavens, which is not a manifest revelation of the principle of the Changes? Moreover, Heaven is simply yin and yang, and yin and yang are simply transformation. Through the friction and agitation of the firm and the yielding, transformation resides in the Changes; taking this to look up and observe the heavens, can its principle not be seen? The forming of images in the heavens is one and the same: from their striking and clashing to become thunder and lightning, to their harmonizing and spreading to become wind and rain—now rousing the primordial qi and making wondrous its power of vigorous swiftness, now moistening the myriad things and extending universally its beneficence of gentle harmony—the ways by which they stir the mechanism of transformation and revive the multitude of moving creatures are thus different. Yet thunder and lightning are the righteous qi of yin and yang, and wind and rain are the benevolent qi of yin and yang; it is as though something presides over them, though one simply cannot perceive its trace—how is any of this not the principle of the Changes rousing and moistening them? From their shining brightly to become the sun and moon, to their alternating and changing to become cold and heat—now adhering to the heavens to illuminate universally, with constancy in their waxing, waning, fullness, and emptiness, now moving in alternation with the seasons, without disorder in their coming, going, and shifting—the ways by which they continue the succession of brightness and bring to completion the work of the year are thus varied. Yet the sun and moon are yin and yang mutually storing their essence, and cold and heat are yin and yang smoothly unfolding their sequence; it is as though a mechanism moves them, though one simply cannot find its beginning—…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
何莫非易理有以推行之乎是可見造化者易
書之法象而易書者造化之實理大哉易也其
誠足以體天之撰者歟而以卜筮小之者陋矣
蓋易非出於聖人之私智也天地有自然之易
聖人不過模寫以成之耳然必有聖人之心易
斯可以盡作易之妙不然則如潛虛洞極太玄
卦氣以之擬易其果有得於易否耶善學者得
之於言語象數之外焉斯其於易也深矣
書
===
帝曰俞允若茲嘉言罔攸伏野無遺賢萬
邦咸寧稽于衆舍己從人不虐無告不
廢困窮惟帝時克
邵元亨
同考試官敎諭譚　批〔知歸重克艱而詞復簡潔可誦〕
錄之以式
考試官敎諭孫　批〔剴切有裨治道非苟作者〕
考試官敎授黃　批〔雅飭有文〕
聖君推克艱之效必舉其事而歸之前聖焉夫
punctuated:
何莫非易理有以推行之乎？是可見造化者，《易》書之法象；而《易》書者，造化之實理。大哉《易》也！其誠足以體天之撰者歟！而以卜筮小之者，陋矣。蓋《易》非出於聖人之私智也，天地有自然之《易》，聖人不過模寫以成之耳。然必有聖人之心《易》，斯可以盡作《易》之妙。不然，則如《潛虛》、《洞極》、《太玄》、《卦氣》，以之擬《易》，其果有得於《易》否耶？善學者，得之於言語象數之外焉，斯其於《易》也深矣。

《書》

「帝曰：『俞！允若茲，嘉言罔攸伏，野無遺賢，萬邦咸寧。稽于衆，舍己從人，不虐無告，不廢困窮，惟帝時克。』」
邵元亨
同考試官敎諭譚　批：〔知歸重克艱，而詞復簡潔可誦。〕錄之以式。
考試官敎諭孫　批：〔剴切有裨治道，非苟作者。〕
考試官敎授黃　批：〔雅飭有文。〕

聖君推克艱之效，必舉其事而歸之前聖焉。夫
translation_en:
…how could any of it not be impelled and carried out by the principles of the Changes? From this it can be seen that the creative transformations of nature are the model images of the Book of Changes (Yishu), and the Book of Changes is the substantial principle of nature's creative transformations. Great indeed is the Changes! Truly, it suffices to embody the workings of Heaven! Those who belittle it as mere divination are narrow-minded. For the Changes did not spring from the private intellect of the sages; Heaven and Earth possess a spontaneous Changes of their own, and the sages did nothing more than depict it to bring the work to completion. Yet one must possess the "Changes of the mind" of the sages before one can exhaust the subtlety of creating the Changes. Otherwise, works such as the Classic of Hidden Emptiness (Qianxu), the Extreme of Penetration (Dongji), the Canon of Supreme Mystery (Taixuan), and the Hexagram Breaths (Guaqi) were all composed in imitation of the Changes—did they truly grasp anything of the Changes or not? Those who excel at learning grasp it beyond words, images, and numbers; thus their understanding of the Changes is profound indeed.

Book of Documents (Shu)

"The Emperor said: 'Yes! If it is truly like this, then admirable words will nowhere be hidden, no worthy men will be left neglected in the wilds, and the myriad states will all enjoy peace. To consult with the multitude, to set aside one's own views and follow others, not to oppress the helpless, and not to neglect the distressed and impoverished—only the Emperor was able to do this.'"
Shao Yuanheng 邵元亨
Comment by Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Tan: [He knows to place the main emphasis on overcoming difficulties, and his phrasing is moreover concise, clean, and worthy of recitation.] Recorded to serve as a model.
Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Sun: [Incisive and beneficial to the way of governance; not a careless composition.]
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang: [Refined, disciplined, and literary.]

When the sage ruler extends the efficacy of overcoming difficulties, he necessarily cites the actual deeds thereof and attributes them to the former sage. Now…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
克艱之效至大也顧其事有不易能者非帝堯
其誰與歸舜因禹之謨而推廣之曰予之紹堯
而治也方思盛治之難繼而君道之難盡也汝
以克艱之謨進焉誠哉契予心矣予特患茲道
之未易能耳信能上下勤恤而罔或不艱焉則
豈特政之乂焉而已乎民之化焉而已乎以茲
集謀猷而言其罔伏矣以茲登俊乂而賢其無
遺矣以茲康民生而萬邦其咸若矣夫人懷其
善而欲兼收之難也必其虛以稽衆卽舍己無
===
吝焉此言所以罔伏也民生至衆而欲舉安之
難也必其惠以恤下卽無告弗傷焉此民所以
咸寧也賢才無盡而欲翕受之難也必其公以
明揚卽困窮必及焉此賢所以無遺也由其效
之大以思其事之艱艱可知矣誰則能之惟帝
焉耳蓋其智如神矣故克以集衆思而致賢良
總章師錫之風可想也其仁如天矣故克以安
兆民而和萬邦其咨俾乂之懷可想也帝誠克
艱厥后矣乎則事既克盡而效有弗臻也哉噫
punctuated: 克艱之效至大也，顧其事有不易能者，非帝堯其誰與歸？舜因禹之謨而推廣之，曰：予之紹堯而治也，方思盛治之難繼，而君道之難盡也。汝以克艱之謨進焉，誠哉契予心矣，予特患茲道之未易能耳。信能上下勤恤，而罔或不艱焉，則豈特政之乂焉而已乎？民之化焉而已乎？以茲集謀猷，而言其罔伏矣；以茲登俊乂，而賢其無遺矣；以茲康民生，而萬邦其咸若矣。夫人懷其善，而欲兼收之，難也；必其虛以稽衆，卽舍己無吝焉，此言所以罔伏也。民生至衆，而欲舉安之，難也；必其惠以恤下，卽無告弗傷焉，此民所以咸寧也。賢才無盡，而欲翕受之，難也；必其公以明揚，卽困窮必及焉，此賢所以無遺也。由其效之大，以思其事之艱，艱可知矣。誰則能之？惟帝焉耳。蓋其智如神矣，故克以集衆思而致賢良，總章、師錫之風可想也；其仁如天矣，故克以安兆民而和萬邦，其咨、俾乂之懷可想也。帝誠克艱厥后矣乎！則事既克盡，而效有弗臻也哉？噫！
translation_en:
… the effects of realizing the difficulties of rule are supremely great; yet the tasks involved are not easy to accomplish—if not to Emperor Yao, to whom could they be attributed?

Shun, building upon Yu's counsel and expanding on it, said: In succeeding Yao to govern, I am just reflecting on how difficult it is to continue his flourishing rule and how hard it is to fulfill the Way of the ruler. You have presented the counsel of realizing the difficulties—truly, this accords with my own heart! I only worry that this Way is not easy to practice. If indeed ruler and ministers above and below can be diligent and solicitous, never failing to recognize the difficulties, then would the result merely be that government is well-ordered, or merely that the people are transformed? By this means we shall gather counsels and plans, so that no good words remain hidden; by this means we shall advance men of eminent talent, so that no worthy is left behind; by this means we shall bring peace to the people's livelihood, so that all the myriad states will be in harmony.

Now, each person cherishes his own goodness, and to gather and adopt it from all of them is difficult; one must be open-minded to consult the multitude, not grudging even to set aside one's own views—this is why no good words remain hidden. The people are most numerous, and to bring peace to every one of them is difficult; one must be benevolent in showing compassion to those below, not harming even the helpless who have no one to appeal to—this is why the people all enjoy peace. Worthies and talents are inexhaustible, and to receive and unite them all is difficult; one must be impartial in openly promoting them, reaching even those in distress and poverty—this is why no worthy is left behind.

When we reflect upon the difficulty of the tasks in light of the greatness of their effects, how arduous they are becomes clear! Who, then, is capable of this? Only the Emperor [Yao] alone. For his wisdom was like that of a spirit, and thus he was able to gather the thoughts of the multitude and attract the worthy and good—one can well imagine his manner of illuminating all the people and receiving the multitude's nomination [of Shun]. His benevolence was like that of Heaven, and thus he was able to give peace to the millions of people and harmonize the myriad states—one can well imagine his concern in sighing over distress and commissioning someone to bring order. Truly, did not the Emperor realize the difficulties of being sovereign! And once the tasks were fully accomplished, how could the effects fail to be achieved? Alas, …

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
吾固于舜之稱堯而得其克艱之心矣然是道
也虛己其要也易咸之象曰君子以虛受人蓋
能虛己則能親賢而愛民治道其易易矣故孟
子論好善優於天下至稱舜之大亦曰舍己從
人焉然則二聖之克艱其有所本哉
明王愼德四夷咸賓無有遠邇畢獻方物
惟服食器用
越應甲
同考試官教諭譚　批　講遠人歸德有照應無費詞讀
===
之爽然
考試官教諭孫　批　義精詞雅
考試官教授黃　批　明當
明王謹德以致遠而貢無異物焉蓋服遠之本
在德也明王愼之而遠人之貢無異物焉此可
以觀德化矣召公舉之以告武王也謂夫王者
以一身爲華夷之主其何修以綏中國撫四夷
哉亦惟端吾身孚化之本而已盍觀之明王乎
夫謂之明王則語其德德之盛也而允迪已至
punctuated:
吾固于舜之稱堯，而得其克艱之心矣。然是道也，虛己其要也。《易》〈咸〉之《象》曰：「君子以虛受人。」蓋能虛己，則能親賢而愛民，治道其易易矣。故孟子論好善優於天下，至稱舜之大，亦曰「舍己從人」焉。然則二聖之克艱，其有所本哉！

「明王愼德，四夷咸賓，無有遠邇，畢獻方物，惟服食器用。」
越應甲
同考試官教諭譚　批：講遠人歸德有照應，無費詞，讀之爽然。
考試官教諭孫　批：義精詞雅。
考試官教授黃　批：明當。

明王謹德以致遠，而貢無異物焉。蓋服遠之本在德也，明王愼之，而遠人之貢無異物焉，此可以觀德化矣。召公舉之以告武王也，謂夫王者以一身爲華夷之主，其何修以綏中國、撫四夷哉？亦惟端吾身孚化之本而已。盍觀之明王乎？夫謂之明王，則語其德，德之盛也，而允迪已至；
translation_en:
Indeed, from Shun's praise of Yao, I have grasped his mind capable of appreciating the difficulty of rulership. Yet as for this Way, humbling oneself is its essential point. The Image commentary on the hexagram Xian ("Influence") in the Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The noble man receives others with humility." For if one can humble oneself, one can draw close to the worthy and love the people, and the Way of governance becomes quite easy. Thus, when Mencius (Mengzi) discussed how a fondness for goodness is more than sufficient to govern the Empire, upon praising the greatness of Shun, he likewise said that he "set aside his own views to follow others." If so, then the capacity of the two sages to appreciate the difficulties of their office surely had its foundation!

"When the enlightened king is cautious about his virtue, the four barbarian tribes all come as guests; whether far or near, all offer up their local products—solely articles of clothing, food, and implements for use."

Yue Yingjia 越應甲

Associate Examiner and Instructor Tan 譚 comments: The exposition on distant peoples turning toward virtue is well-coordinated and free of wasted words; reading it is refreshing.
Examiner and Instructor Sun 孫 comments: The meaning is precise and the diction elegant.
Examiner and Professor Huang 黃 comments: Clear and fitting.

The enlightened king carefully attends to his virtue so as to draw in distant peoples, and their tribute includes no strange rarities. For the root of winning over the distant lies in virtue; when the enlightened king is cautious about it, the tribute of distant peoples includes no strange rarities—from this one may observe the transformative power of virtue. The Duke of Shao (Shao Gong) cited this to counsel King Wu, meaning to say: Since a true king in his single person serves as lord of both Chinese and barbarians, what should he cultivate in order to give repose to the Central States and pacify the four barbarian tribes? It is simply a matter of rectifying in one's own person the foundation of sincere transformation. Why not look at the enlightened kings of old? Now, to be called an enlightened king means that, speaking of his virtue, his virtue is abundant, and his sincere practice of it has reached the utmost;…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
然語其心心之純也而祗慎不忘故大德不踰
矣猶恐聰明或壅於遐邇而惕乎其防必使德
足作孚而爲天下所胥向焉巳也懋德克勤矣
猶恐意念或雜於玩好而兢乎其守必使德足
作肅而毋爲遠入所窺焉巳也惟慎德如是吾
知維皇建極而中外之勢以一則雖四夷殊疆
而罔不率服矣以德服人而遠近之情斯聯則
雖四夷殊俗而莫不來享矣德明而懷者賓焉
非不以方物獻也然其所獻者惟服食也取其
===
昭事上之忱而巳何也知明王服食之外無他
尚也德威而畏者賓焉非不以方物獻也然其
所獻者惟器用也取其將享上之敬而巳何也
知明王器用之外無他好也故觀明王之所慎
又觀慎德之所致者則今日旅獒之貢從古未
有也而受之恐遠人窺吾淺深矣可不慎與抑
慎德者王道大本不獨服遠係焉然必明以察
其幾而後能慎也前乎丹書後乎旅獒皆慎微
之炯戒也非遇明聖其孰察之故曰兢兢業業
punctuated: 然語其心，心之純也，而祗慎不忘。故大德不踰矣，猶恐聰明或壅於遐邇，而惕乎其防，必使德足作孚，而爲天下所胥向焉巳也；懋德克勤矣，猶恐意念或雜於玩好，而兢乎其守，必使德足作肅，而毋爲遠入所窺焉巳也。惟慎德如是，吾知維皇建極，而中外之勢以一，則雖四夷殊疆，而罔不率服矣；以德服人，而遠近之情斯聯，則雖四夷殊俗，而莫不來享矣。德明而懷者賓焉，非不以方物獻也，然其所獻者惟服食也，取其昭事上之忱而巳。何也？知明王服食之外無他尚也。德威而畏者賓焉，非不以方物獻也，然其所獻者惟器用也，取其將享上之敬而巳。何也？知明王器用之外無他好也。故觀明王之所慎，又觀慎德之所致者，則今日旅獒之貢，從古未有也。而受之，恐遠人窺吾淺深矣，可不慎與？抑慎德者，王道大本，不獨服遠係焉，然必明以察其幾而後能慎也。前乎《丹書》，後乎《旅獒》，皆慎微之炯戒也。非遇明聖，其孰察之？故曰「兢兢業業」
translation_en: … Yet speaking of his heart, his heart is pure, and he is reverently cautious without forgetting. Therefore, although he does not transgress in great virtue, he still fears that his hearing and sight might be blocked regarding the near and the distant, and so he is vigilant in his precautions, ensuring that his virtue is sufficient to inspire trust and be turned toward by all under heaven, and nothing more. Although he is able to be diligent in cultivating lofty virtue, he still fears that his thoughts and intentions might be mixed with a fondness for curiosities, and so he is circumspect in his self-guarding, ensuring that his virtue is sufficient to inspire reverence and not be spied upon for weaknesses by people from afar [reading 遠入 as 遠人], and nothing more. Only when he is cautious about his virtue like this do I know that the Sovereign establishes the standard of perfection and the momentum of the central lands and the outside is thereby unified—so that even though the Four Barbarians have different territories, there are none who do not follow and submit; and that by subduing men through virtue, the sentiments of the distant and the near are thus connected—so that even though the Four Barbarians have different customs, there are none who do not come to present offerings. When his virtue is illustrious and those who cherish it come as guests, it is not that they fail to present local tribute; yet what they present is only clothing and food, chosen merely to display their sincerity in serving their superior. Why is this? Because they know that an enlightened king values nothing else beyond clothing and food. When his virtue is awesome and those who stand in awe of it come as guests, it is not that they fail to present local tribute; yet what they present is only vessels and utensils for use, chosen merely to convey their respect in making offerings to their superior. Why is this? Because they know that an enlightened king has no other fondness beyond vessels and utensils for use. Therefore, if we observe what the enlightened kings were cautious about, and also observe what was brought about by their caution in virtue, then today's tribute of the hound of the Lü (Lü ao) is something unprecedented since antiquity. And if you accept it, I fear that distant people will spy out our depth and shallowness—how can one not be cautious? Moreover, being cautious about virtue is the great foundation of the Kingly Way; not only does the submission of the distant depend upon it, yet one must first be enlightened enough to discern its subtle incipient tendencies before one can be cautious. Earlier, the Cinnabar Writing (Dan shu), and later, the "Hounds of Lü" (Lü ao), were both bright warnings about being cautious in small matters. Unless they met with an enlightened sage, who could discern them? Therefore, when it is said, "cautious and trembling" …

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
者言愼也曰知幾其神者言明也召公論愼德
而歸之明王也其指深哉
詩
百辟卿士媚于天子不解于位民之攸墍
錢潮
同考試官教諭譚　批　雅而優中有奇氣講不解處尤切
本官孟深於詩學者
考試官教諭孫　批　模寫忠愛之心殆盡
考試官教授黃　批　理正詞婉錄之
===
詩人願諸臣之效忠于君而久道以安民也蓋
民安則天下安也而臣子以是望君其忠矣哉
宜詩人爲後王願也且夫世不常治而時尤易
失此盛世君臣常相儆而精神常相通也是故
修德任賢而綱紀四方君既勤而民亦墍矣乃
百辟卿士猶以爲國之危也由于民之勞也而
民之勞也由于上之懈也故臣之心常切于君
而憂盛危明以用其愛則必使君之心常通于
民而持盈保太以圖其終居至尊之地則志意
punctuated:
者，言愼也；曰「知幾其神」者，言明也。召公論愼德而歸之明王也，其指深哉！

詩
「百辟卿士，媚于天子。不解于位，民之攸墍。」
錢潮
同考試官教諭譚　批：雅而優，中有奇氣，講「不解」處尤切。
本官孟：深於《詩》學者。
考試官教諭孫　批：模寫忠愛之心殆盡。
考試官教授黃　批：理正詞婉，錄之。

詩人願諸臣之效忠于君，而久道以安民也。蓋民安則天下安也，而臣子以是望君，其忠矣哉！宜詩人爲後王願也。且夫世不常治，而時尤易失，此盛世君臣常相儆而精神常相通也。是故修德任賢，而綱紀四方，君既勤而民亦墍矣。乃百辟卿士猶以爲國之危也，由于民之勞也；而民之勞也，由于上之懈也。故臣之心常切于君，而憂盛危明以用其愛；則必使君之心常通于民，而持盈保太以圖其終。居至尊之地，則志意
translation_en:
… speaks of caution; and the saying "To know the subtle incipient tendencies is divine" speaks of perspicacity. When the Duke of Shao discussed being cautious of virtue and attributed it to the perspicacious king, how profound was his meaning!

Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
"All the feudal lords and high ministers show loving devotion to the Son of Heaven; / Neverremiss in his position, it is he in whom the people find rest."
Qian Chao
Associate Examiner, Instructor Tan, comments: Refined and accomplished, with an extraordinary vitality within; the exposition of the passage on "never remiss" is especially pertinent.
This official, Meng, comments: One who is profound in the scholarship of the Classic of Poetry.
Examiner, Instructor Sun, comments: It portrays the heart of loyalty and affection almost to perfection.
Examiner, Professor Huang, comments: The reasoning is upright and the phrasing is graceful; record it.

The poet wishes for all the ministers to devote their loyalty to their ruler, so that he may long abide in the Way to give rest to the people. Indeed, when the people are at rest, the realm is at rest; when ministers and subjects hope for this from their ruler, how loyal they are! Rightly did the poet wish this for the sovereigns of later ages. Moreover, the world is not perpetually well-governed, and opportunity is especially easy to lose; this is why in a flourishing age ruler and ministers constantly admonish one another and their spirits are constantly in communion. Therefore, in cultivating virtue, employing the worthy, and giving laws and order to the four quarters, when the ruler has been diligent, the people too have found rest. Yet all the feudal lords and high ministers still consider that peril to the state arises from the toil of the people, and the toil of the people arises from the remissness of the sovereign above. Thus, the hearts of the ministers are ever earnestly devoted to their ruler, being anxious in times of prosperity and fearful in an age of enlightenment as they exercise their affection; they must ensure that the heart of the ruler is ever in communion with the people, preserving fullness and safeguarding supreme peace so as to secure the end. Occupying the position of supreme veneration, one's will and intentions…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
易肆威儀聲譽得如始乎惟願君勿懈于進修
也而令聞令望昭然如天地之不息當衆欲之
攻則間隙易乗幸由羣匹果如初乎惟願君勿
懈于延攬也而無怨無惡顯然如日月之無私
王心常覺而四海之内可以坐照不慇不忘所
以衽席我生民者與君福相無疆矣微臣何幸
而永承夫燕及之休耶聖心常流而萬邦之遠
可以默化爲綱爲紀所以寘安我黎庶者與君
身相盜謚矣微臣何修而來�World夫太平之盛耶
===
===
是蓋君民相爲感通而天人相爲默應君志定
而民心安民心安而天命固此忠臣愛君之至
而後王莫大之福也吾王宜民宜人之治萬年
一日矣抑鳬鷖假樂古人燕樂之章也其始曰
宜民宜人其末曰不懈曰攸塈成周所以爲有
道之長者心乎民也苟不心乎民而徒慕不懈
之名則若衡石程書衞士傳餐者亦謂之能保
治乎
昊天有成命二后受之成王不敢康夙夜
punctuated:
易肆，威儀聲譽得如始乎？惟願君勿懈于進修也，而令聞令望昭然如天地之不息；當衆欲之攻，則間隙易乗，幸由羣匹果如初乎？惟願君勿懈于延攬也，而無怨無惡顯然如日月之無私。王心常覺，而四海之内可以坐照，不慇不忘，所以衽席我生民者，與君福相無疆矣，微臣何幸而永承夫燕及之休耶！聖心常流，而萬邦之遠可以默化，爲綱爲紀，所以寘安我黎庶者，與君身相盜謚矣，微臣何修而來World夫太平之盛耶！是蓋君民相爲感通，而天人相爲默應。君志定而民心安，民心安而天命固，此忠臣愛君之至，而後王莫大之福也，吾王宜民宜人之治萬年一日矣。抑《鳬鷖》、《假樂》，古人燕樂之章也。其始曰「宜民宜人」，其末曰「不懈」、曰「攸塈」，成周所以爲有道之長者，心乎民也。苟不心乎民，而徒慕不懈之名，則若衡石程書、衞士傳餐者，亦謂之能保治乎？

昊天有成命，二后受之，成王不敢康，夙夜
translation_en:
…easily grows unrestrained; can his dignified demeanor and fine reputation remain as they were at the start? They only wish that the ruler not slacken in his self-cultivation, so that his admirable renown and esteemed reputation shine forth like the unceasing operations of Heaven and Earth. When assailed by a multitude of desires, openings are easily exploited; can his following the good and employing his peers truly remain as it was at first? They only wish that the ruler not slacken in drawing in talent, so that his freedom from resentment and malice is as manifest as the impartiality of the sun and moon. When the king's mind is ever awake, all within the Four Seas can be illuminated from his seat; neither erring nor forgetting, the means by which he places our living people upon a comfortable mat will be as boundless as the ruler's own blessings. How fortunate are his humble servants to forever receive the grace that extends tranquility to them! When the sage's mind constantly flows forth, the distant myriad states can be silently transformed; acting as the main cord and themeshes of the net, the means by which he settles our multitude in peace will abide in tranquil serenity [?] alongside the ruler's own person. What virtue have his humble servants cultivated to witness [?] the flourishing of such great peace! This is because ruler and people mutually move and communicate with one another, and Heaven and man silently respond to each other. When the ruler's will is fixed, the people's hearts are at peace; when the people's hearts are at peace, the Mandate of Heaven is secure. This is the utmost of a loyal minister's love for his ruler, and the greatest blessing for asuccessor king; our king's governance that is suitable to the people and suitable to men will endure for ten thousand years as if a single day. Moreover, "Wild Ducks" (Fuyi) and "Admirable and Joyous" (Jiale) are songs of feasting and rejoicing from the ancients. At the beginning it says "suitable to the people, suitable to men," and at the end it says "unremitting" and "a place of rest." The reason the Zhou at its height achieved long-lasting rule under the Way was that its heart was with the people. If a ruler's heart is not with the people, and he merely covets the reputation of being unremitting, then could those who weighed documents by the stone-weight or had guards pass in their meals also be called capable of preserving good governance?

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
基命宥密於緝熙單厥心肆其靖之
任　謨
同考試官教諭譚　批　提掇照應處神彩動人成王保
命氣象宛然見之佳士也
考試官教諭孫　批　莊重爾雅深得頌體
考試官教授黃　批　精當可式
詩人即前王所以承命者而推後王之能保焉
蓋文武以德受命周之盛王也非成王之善守
孰能保哉且夫王者有業以靖天下也其創之
者以心而守之者亦以心心不盡而業斯替矣
我成王之繼二后何如哉蓋天監在下而有命
既集在文王以明德受之于先在武王以明德
受之于后而所以靖之者后人責也惟我成王
念盛美之難繼而每勵夫無逸之衷思治安之
難保而常切夫其勤之念天命無外非隘德可
以基也自夙而夜所以承藉之者其德宏以深
焉天命無間不可以淺德基也自夙而夜所以
負荷之者其德靜以密焉惟其宥也則聰明弗
punctuated:
基命宥密，於緝熙單厥心，肆其靖之。」

任謨

同考試官教諭譚批：提掇照應處，神彩動人，成王保命氣象宛然見之，佳士也。
考試官教諭孫批：莊重爾雅，深得頌體。
考試官教授黃批：精當可式。

詩人即前王所以承命者，而推後王之能保焉。蓋文、武以德受命，周之盛王也；非成王之善守，孰能保哉？且夫王者有業以靖天下也，其創之者以心，而守之者亦以心；心不盡而業斯替矣。我成王之繼二后何如哉？蓋天監在下，而有命既集，在文王以明德受之于先，在武王以明德受之于后，而所以靖之者，后人責也。惟我成王，念盛美之難繼，而每勵夫無逸之衷；思治安之難保，而常切夫其勤之念。天命無外，非隘德可以基也；自夙而夜，所以承藉之者，其德宏以深焉。天命無間，不可以淺德基也；自夙而夜，所以負荷之者，其德靜以密焉。惟其宥也，則聰明弗
translation_en:
… laid the foundation of the Mandate in breadth and stillness. Oh, continuing and making it bright, he exhausted his heart in it, and thus brought it peace.”

Ren Mo 任謨

Comment by Associate Examiner County Director of Studies Tan 譚: Where he raises and echoes the themes, the spirited brilliance is moving. One sees vividly the bearing with which King Cheng preserved the Mandate—a fine scholar!
Comment by Examiner County Director of Studies Sun 孫: Dignified and refined, deeply capturing the style of the Sacrificial Odes (Song 頌).
Comment by Examiner Prefectural Director of Studies Huang 黃: Precise and apt, worthy of serving as a model.

The poet proceeds from how the former kings received the Mandate to extol how the successor king was able to preserve it. For Kings Wen and Wu received the Mandate through their virtue and were the flourishing kings of Zhou; were it not for King Cheng’s skill in safeguarding it, who could have preserved it? Moreover, when a true king possesses a patrimony Whereby to bring peace to All under Heaven, he who founds it does so through his mind-and-heart, and he who safeguards it likewise does so through his mind-and-heart; if the mind-and-heart is not fully exerted, the patrimony thereupon declines. How was it when our King Cheng succeeded the two sovereigns? When Heaven looked down upon the world below and its Mandate had settled upon them, King Wen received it first through his illustrious virtue, and King Wu received it afterward through his illustrious virtue; yet bringing peace to it was the responsibility of their successor. Only our King Cheng, mindful that flourishing beauty is hard to continue, ever spurred on his disposition of untiring diligence; reflecting that peace and order are hard to preserve, he ever held fast to the thought of constant toil. The Mandate of Heaven has nothing outside it and cannot be founded upon narrow virtue; from morning to night, the virtue by which he upheld and rested upon it was vast and deep. The Mandate of Heaven has no pause and cannot be founded upon shallow virtue; from morning to night, the virtue by which he bore its weight was tranquil and dense. Because of its breadth, his intelligence was not…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
予能得其微矣可錄
考試官教諭孫　批　體裁嚴整
考試官教授黃　批　明健
春秋紀霸好而幸有一王之命討焉蓋命討王
者之大權也齊桓兩有奉焉春秋盛不爲周幸
與曷會乎城濮我公與齊桓謀伐衞也曷謀乎
伐衞惠王使召伯廖賜齊桓命而請之也夫王
者法天故五服五章謂之天命非可得私也桓
自管仲相而急于圖霸以尊王實世道所攸賴
者今鞏洛之音渙頒于內史晉錫于王臣而九
===
命之榮桓所顯膺焉是大宗伯所掌者爲天子
命德之大權而西周秬鬯之盛再見矣噫股肱
夾輔之命先王勞之而賜之盟乃後有私相爲
命于蒲者矣何幸桓之奉揚天命乎異日翼戴
藩屏功成九合謂非本于伯廖之一行不可也
王者法天故五刑五用謂之天討非可得私也
衞因子頹之亂而敢于助孼以奸位實人心所
共憤者今濮陽之問肅將于元臣授詞于伯舅
punctuated:
予能得其微矣，可錄。
考試官教諭孫　批：體裁嚴整。
考試官教授黃　批：明健。
《春秋》紀霸好，而幸有一王之命討焉。蓋命討，王者之大權也，齊桓兩有奉焉，《春秋》盛不爲周幸與？曷會乎城濮？我公與齊桓謀伐衞也。曷謀乎伐衞？惠王使召伯廖賜齊桓命而請之也。夫王者法天，故五服五章謂之天命，非可得私也。桓自管仲相，而急于圖霸以尊王，實世道所攸賴者。今鞏洛之音，渙頒于內史，晉錫于王臣，而九命之榮，桓所顯膺焉。是大宗伯所掌者，爲天子命德之大權，而西周秬鬯之盛再見矣。噫！股肱夾輔之命，先王勞之而賜之盟，乃後有私相爲命于蒲者矣。何幸桓之奉揚天命乎！異日翼戴藩屏，功成九合，謂非本于伯廖之一行不可也。王者法天，故五刑五用謂之天討，非可得私也。衞因子頹之亂，而敢于助孼以奸位，實人心所共憤者。今濮陽之問，肅將于元臣，授詞于伯舅，
translation_en:
… [?] has grasped its subtleties; it is worthy of being recorded.
Examiner, Instructor Sun, comments: The structure and style are rigorous and well-ordered.
Examiner, Confucian School Director Huang, comments: Lucid and vigorous.
The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the friendly meetings of the hegemons, yet rejoices that the investiture and punitive expeditions of the one true King are preserved therein. For investiture and punitive expeditions are the great prerogatives of a true king; Duke Huan of Qi (Qi Huan) respectfully upheld both. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals [not — transcribed 盛 for 豈] rejoice on behalf of the Zhou? Why did they meet at Chengpu? Our Duke and Duke Huan of Qi were plotting to attack Wei. Why plot to attack Wei? King Hui (Huiwang) had sent Earl Liao of Shao (Shao Bo Liao) to bestow a royal charge upon Duke Huan of Qi and request that he do so. Now, the true king models himself on Heaven; therefore, the five grades of ceremonial dress with their five emblems are called the Mandate of Heaven, which cannot be appropriated for private ends. Ever since Guan Zhong became his chief minister, Duke Huan was eager to achieve hegemony in order to honor the King—truly something upon which the moral order of the world depended. Now the royal voice from Gong and Luo was grandly proclaimed by the Scribes of the Interior and lavishly bestowed through the King's minister, and the glory of the nine-fold investiture was illustriously received by Huan. Thus, what the Grand Ceremonialist (Da Zongbo) administered was the Son of Heaven's great prerogative of rewarding virtue, and the flourishing splendor of the black-millet aromatic wine of the Western Zhou was seen once again! Alas! As for the charge to serve as limbs and supporting ministers, the former kings rewarded their toil and granted them covenants; yet in later times there were those who privately conferred charges upon one another at Pu. How fortunate it was that Huan respectfully extolled the Mandate of Heaven! In later days, when he supported and shielded the royal house as a feudatory screen and achieved the merit of nine-fold assemblies, one cannot say that it did not originate from this single mission of Earl Liao. The true king models himself on Heaven; therefore, the five punishments with their five applications are called Heaven's punitive expedition, which cannot be appropriated for private ends. Taking advantage of the rebellion of Zitui, Wei dared to aid an evil Pretender in usurping the throne—truly something that provoked the shared indignation of all human hearts. Now, the call to account at Puyang was solemnly conveyed by a senior royal minister, who delivered the charge to the Royal Uncle (Bojiu), …

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
而九伐之法桓其明勑焉是大司馬所掌者爲
天子討罪之大權而西周鈇鉞之盛再見矣噫
五侯九伯之征先王命之而賜之履乃後有矯
之以行私于防者矣何幸桓之奉行天討乎異
日南權西抑業成一匡謂非始于立頹之一問
不可也故書城濮之會而其美彰矣抑桓之奉
玆以往誠有命無咎者而衛胡有甲寅之抗耶
抗齊實抗周也使桓能一鼓得之以請戮於周
則勤王有終矣乃取賂以還不亦上負天子哉
===
此桓之止於霸而周之不復西也
遂伐楚次于陘　楚屈完來盟于師盟于
召陵僖公四年　公會晉侯宋公衛侯曹
伯齊世子光莒子邾子滕子薛伯杞伯
小邾子伐鄭會于蕭魚襄公十一年夏
楚子蔡侯陳侯鄭伯許男徐子滕子頓
子胡子沈子小邾子宋世子佐淮夷會
于申昭公四年
曹衎
punctuated:
而九伐之法，桓其明勑焉。是大司馬所掌者，爲天子討罪之大權，而西周鈇鉞之盛再見矣。噫！五侯九伯之征，先王命之而賜之履，乃後有矯之以行私于防者矣，何幸桓之奉行天討乎！異日南權西抑，業成一匡，謂非始于立頹之一問，不可也。故書「城濮之會」，而其美彰矣。抑桓之奉玆以往，誠有命無咎者，而衛胡有甲寅之抗耶？抗齊實抗周也。使桓能一鼓得之，以請戮於周，則勤王有終矣；乃取賂以還，不亦上負天子哉？此桓之止於霸，而周之不復西也。
遂伐楚，次于陘；楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵（僖公四年）。公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、齊世子光、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子伐鄭，會于蕭魚（襄公十一年夏）。楚子、蔡侯、陳侯、鄭伯、許男、徐子、滕子、頓子、胡子、沈子、小邾子、宋世子佐、淮夷會于申（昭公四年）。
曹衎
translation_en:
…and the laws of the nine punitive expeditions were clearly commanded to Duke Huan. Thus what the Minister of War held in his charge was the Son of Heaven's great authority to punish the guilty, and the flourishing grandeur of the battle-axes of the Western Zhou was seen once again. Alas! The campaigns of the five marquises and nine earls had been commanded by the former kings when they bestowed the boundaries of authority, yet later there were those who falsified this mandate to pursue private ends at Fang—how fortunate it was that Duke Huan respectfully carried out the punishment of Heaven! When in later days he checked the south and restrained the west, accomplishing the enterprise of uniting and rectifying the realm, one cannot say that it did not begin with this single inquiry into the enthronement of Zitui. Therefore the Annals record "the meeting at Chengpu," and its excellence is made manifest. Yet since Duke Huan went forth bearing this mandate, truly possessing a charge free from fault, why did Wei offer resistance on the jiayin day? To resist Qi was in fact to resist Zhou. Had Duke Huan been able to capture them at the first drumbeat and request their execution by Zhou, then his service to the King would have been brought to completion; instead, he accepted bribes and withdrew—did this not fail the Son of Heaven above? This is why Duke Huan stopped at being merely a hegemon, and why Zhou never again returned to the west.

"[They] thereupon invaded Chu and halted at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army, and made a covenant at Shaoling" (fourth year of Duke Xi). "The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Heir Apparent Guang of Qi, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Little Zhu to invade Zheng; [they] met at Xiaoyu" (summer, eleventh year of Duke Xiang). "The Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Cai, the Marquis of Chen, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Viscount of Xu, the Viscount of Teng, the Viscount of Dun, the Viscount of Hu, the Viscount of Shen, the Viscount of Little Zhu, Heir Apparent Zuo of Song, and the Huai Yi met at Shen" (fourth year of Duke Zhao).

By Cao Kan 曹衎.

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導孫　批　桓悼不戰之功殆伯而王者也
足作模寫婉切錄之
考試官教諭孫　批　詞勁意明可取
考試官教授黃　批　深得傳意
春秋美二霸不戰之功以其近王事也甚矣王
者以不戰爲威也桓之攘夷悼之服貳有焉春
秋所以美之與蓋嘗於欒書桑隧之役而有感
於二霸之功矣夫齊桓之創伯也事孰大於制
楚者使徒制以力則吾力竭而二廣之虎視猶
故也乃桓之伐楚也兵威已震于南海矣則用
敬仲之謀而戰之不遑陘亭駐師而修以文告
也徼與同好也豈以八國之全力而畏一楚哉
誠不忍以吾節制之民而輕於一擊也果而屈
完服義退三十里卒有召陵之款焉則九合之
盛此其先聲矣楊子謂春秋美召陵其在斯乎
晉悼之復伯也事孰大於服鄭者使徒服以力
則吾力疲而二境之狐疑未釋也乃悼之伐鄭
也兵力大振于東門矣則從伯駢之請而信之
punctuated:
同考試官訓導孫　批：桓、悼不戰之功，殆伯而王者也。足作模寫婉切，錄之。
考試官教諭孫　批：詞勁意明，可取。
考試官教授黃　批：深得傳意。

《春秋》美二霸不戰之功，以其近王事也。甚矣！王者以不戰爲威也。桓之攘夷，悼之服貳，有焉；《春秋》所以美之與？蓋嘗於欒書桑隧之役，而有感於二霸之功矣。夫齊桓之創伯也，事孰大於制楚者？使徒制以力，則吾力竭，而二廣之虎視猶故也。乃桓之伐楚也，兵威已震于南海矣，則用敬仲之謀，而戰之不遑。陘亭駐師，而修以文告也，徼與同好也。豈以八國之全力，而畏一楚哉？誠不忍以吾節制之民，而輕於一擊也。果而屈完服義，退三十里，卒有召陵之款焉。則九合之盛，此其先聲矣。楊子謂「《春秋》美召陵」，其在斯乎！晉悼之復伯也，事孰大於服鄭者？使徒服以力，則吾力疲，而二境之狐疑未釋也。乃悼之伐鄭也，兵力大振于東門矣，則從伯駢之請，而信之
translation_en:
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Sun, comments: The achievements of Dukes Huan and Dao in winning without fighting are nearly those of hegemons acting as true kings. This piece depicts the matter with tactful precision; record it for inclusion.
Examiner, Instructor Sun, comments: The diction is vigorous and the meaning clear; it is worthy of selection.
Examiner, Instructor Huang, comments: It deeply captures the meaning of the commentary.

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) praises the achievements of the two hegemons in winning without fighting because their actions approached the way of a true king. Great indeed is the way a true king uses non-combat as his awe-inspiring might! Duke Huan's repelling of the barbarians and Duke Dao's winning over of the disaffected both possessed this quality; is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals praised them? Looking back at Luan Shu's campaign at Sangsui, one is moved to reflect upon the achievements of these two hegemons. When Duke Huan of Qi first established his hegemony, what enterprise was greater than restraining Chu? Had he sought to restrain them merely by force, our own strength would have been exhausted, while the tiger-like glare of Chu's "Two Broad" chariot divisions would have remained as fierce as ever. Instead, when Duke Huan attacked Chu, once his military might had already shaken the southern seas, he adopted the counsel of Jingzhong [Guan Zhong] and refrained from rushing into battle. Halting his army at Xingting, he cultivated relations through diplomatic pronouncements and sought to share in friendly amity. How could it be that, possessing the combined might of eight states, he feared a single state of Chu? Truly, he could not bear to take his own well-disciplined people and lightly risk them in a single strike. Sure enough, Qu Wan submitted to righteousness; the army withdrew thirty li, and ultimately the covenant of peace at Shaoling was concluded. Thus, for the grand achievement of assembling the lords nine times, this was the herald. When Master Yang [Yang Xiong] said that "the Spring and Autumn Annals praises Shaoling," did he not mean this very thing? When Duke Dao of Jin restored the hegemony, what enterprise was greater than winning over Zheng? Had he sought to win them over merely by force, our own strength would have been worn out, while the suspicions along the two borders would have remained unresolved. Instead, when Duke Dao attacked Zheng, once his military strength had been grandly displayed at the Eastern Gate, he heeded the request of Bopian and trusted…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
舉一國而皆盡其道可以言順矣夫一國惟君
與臣也君臣盡道而順之達于國也詎不信哉
記禮者意謂國以大順爲治順以盡道爲極是
故自身而家其肥固各有所指矣至于國也何
如彼大臣所以表率百僚者也非法無以貞度
茲則翼翼乎奉一人之道揆而不法者無有矣
小臣所以分理百職者也非廉無以觀守茲則
兢兢乎秉一心之精白而不廉者無有矣官職
異等也而有式序之典不陵不援無相越矣非
寅恭推讓之風乎君臣異位也而有相正之義
惟令惟共無相比矣非明良吁咈之盛乎斯則
職業克修而形迹罔間君臣交儆而精神常通
非國之肥而何哉吾知觀政在朝而一德旣爲
之咸有則觀化於國而運祚自見其豐隆國有
元氣非人不固令惟各盡其道則培養有人所
以爲元氣之周流者何其盛滿而不窮乎國有
神氣非人不張令惟各率其職則護持者衆所
以爲神氣之振揚者何其充足而有餘乎是雖
punctuated: 舉一國而皆盡其道，可以言順矣。夫一國，惟君與臣也。君臣盡道，而順之達于國也，詎不信哉？記禮者意謂：國以大順爲治，順以盡道爲極。是故自身而家，其肥固各有所指矣。至于國也，何如？彼大臣，所以表率百僚者也，非法無以貞度；茲則翼翼乎奉一人之道揆，而不法者無有矣。小臣，所以分理百職者也，非廉無以觀守；茲則兢兢乎秉一心之精白，而不廉者無有矣。官職異等也，而有式序之典，不陵不援，無相越矣，非寅恭推讓之風乎？君臣異位也，而有相正之義，惟令惟共，無相比矣，非明良吁咈之盛乎？斯則職業克修而形迹罔間，君臣交儆而精神常通，非國之肥而何哉？吾知觀政在朝，而一德旣爲之咸有；則觀化於國，而運祚自見其豐隆。國有元氣，非人不固；令惟各盡其道，則培養有人，所以爲元氣之周流者，何其盛滿而不窮乎？國有神氣，非人不張；令惟各率其職，則護持者衆，所以爲神氣之振揚者，何其充足而有餘乎？是雖
translation_en:
When an entire state fulfills its proper way, one may speak of harmony. Now, an entire state consists simply of ruler and ministers. When ruler and ministers fulfill their proper way, harmony extends throughout the state—how could this be doubted?

The recorder of the Rites meant to say that a state takes great harmony as its order, and harmony takes the fulfillment of the proper way as its ultimate standard. Therefore, from the personal self to the family, what constitutes their "richness" (fei) certainly has its specific referent in each case. When it comes to the state, what is it like?

Those great ministers are the ones who set an example for the hundred officials; without lawfulness, there is no way to rectify institutional norms. Here, however, they reverently uphold the moral standard of the One Man [the ruler], and there are none who are unlawful. The lesser ministers are the ones who divide and manage the hundred duties; without integrity, there is no way to observe their probity. Here, however, they cautiously hold fast to the pure whiteness of a single mind, and there are none who lack integrity. Official posts differ in rank, yet there are canons of proper sequence; neither overstepping those above nor clinging to those below, they do not transgress against one another—is this not the custom of reverent courtesy and mutual yielding? Ruler and ministers differ in position, yet there is the duty of mutual correction; whether commanding or obeying, they do not form partisan cliques with one another—is this not the flourishing of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers expressing agreement and dissent ("alas" and "nay")? Thus, official duties are capably cultivated without estrangement in outward form, and ruler and ministers mutually admonish one another while their spirit remains in constant communion—what is this if not the richness of the state?

I know that if one observes governance in the court and sees that pure virtue is already possessed by all, then when one observes transformation in the state, its destiny and blessings will naturally appear abundant and prosperous. A state possesses primordial vitality (yuanqi), which cannot be secured without men; now[?], since each fulfills his proper way, there are men to nurture it—how full and inexhaustible is the circulation of this primordial vitality! A state possesses spiritual vitality (shenqi), which cannot be expanded without men; now[?], since each follows his official duty, there are many to protect and uphold it—how sufficient and abundant is the rousing and uplifting of this spiritual vitality! title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
不外乎一家之椎而宗社無疆之命脉此其益
培雖未達於九有之廣而天下和平之氣象此
其已裕以此觀順順可知也君子原其始治情
之功不誣矣雖然君心者順之本也化之原也
古昔聖人以純王之心發爲純王之政不但國
治而天地官萬物育者不期順而順也苟出之
無本而有意於爲順則制作紛紛適以長戾於
國矣如天下何故曰有天德便可語王道
綦民不作諸侯賔服兵革不試五刑不用
百姓無患天子不怒如此則樂達矣
===
郁德據
考試官敎諭孫　批　太和景象宛於篇中見之是知
樂之深者
考試官敎授黃　批　典則春容
惟天下咸安見樂之所由通也甚矣樂未易言
也即天下之相安而和德著矣樂其有不達哉
記樂記者蓋謂惟至和而後可以語樂惟至和
之通乎人心而後可以語達吾謂樂至則無怨
punctuated:
不外乎一家之椎，而宗社無疆之命脉，此其益培；雖未達於九有之廣，而天下和平之氣象，此其已裕。以此觀順，順可知也；君子原其始，治情之功不誣矣。雖然，君心者，順之本也，化之原也。古昔聖人以純王之心，發爲純王之政，不但國治，而天地官、萬物育者，不期順而順也。苟出之無本，而有意於爲順，則制作紛紛，適以長戾於國矣，如天下何？故曰：「有天德，便可語王道。」

綦民不作，諸侯賔服，兵革不試，五刑不用，百姓無患，天子不怒，如此則樂達矣。
郁德據
考試官敎諭孫　批：太和景象，宛於篇中見之，是知樂之深者。
考試官敎授黃　批：典則春容。

惟天下咸安，見樂之所由通也。甚矣，樂未易言也！即天下之相安，而和德著矣，樂其有不達哉？記《樂記》者蓋謂：惟至和而後可以語樂，惟至和之通乎人心而後可以語達。吾謂樂至則無怨⋯⋯
translation_en:
…does not go beyond the inferring [? 椎 for 推] from a single family, yet the boundless lifeblood of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain is thereby increasingly nurtured; although it has not yet reached across the breadth of the nine regions, the atmosphere of peace and harmony throughout the realm is thereby already abundant. Observing harmony and obedience in this way, obedience can be known; when the gentleman traces its origins, the merit of governing human feelings is proven true. Even so, the ruler's mind is the root of obedience and the source of transformation. The sages of antiquity, taking the mind of a pure true king, manifested it as the governance of a pure true king; not only was the state well-governed, but heaven and earth fulfilled their functions and the myriad things flourished—achieving harmony and obedience without deliberately seeking to do so. If it issues forth without a root, and one intentionally strives to manufacture obedience, then institutions and measures will proliferate in confusion, serving only to foster perversity in the state—what then can be done for the realm? Therefore it is said: "Only when one possesses heavenly virtue can one speak of the Kingly Way."

"When violent [? 綦 for 暴] people do not arise, the feudal lords submit as guests, weapons and armor are not put to use, the five punishments are not applied, the common people suffer no calamities, and the Son of Heaven shows no anger—when it is like this, then music has prevailed throughout."
Yu Deju 郁德據
Examiner, County Director of Studies Sun 孫, comments: The vision of supreme harmony is vividly seen throughout this essay; this is someone who understands music deeply.
Examiner, Prefectural Director of Studies Huang 黃, comments: Classical in standard, serene and unhurried in style.

Only when all under heaven are universally at peace can one see whereby music penetrates everywhere. Indeed, music is not easy to speak of! By the very fact that all under heaven dwell in mutual peace, the virtue of harmony is made manifest—how could music fail to prevail throughout? In recording the Record of Music (Yueji 樂記), the writer meant to say: Only when there is supreme harmony can one speak of music, and only when supreme harmony penetrates human hearts can one speak of its prevailing throughout. When I say that "when music reaches its culmination there is no resentment"…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
者何以徵之蓋樂也者暴戾可化兵刑可弭上
下可和者也一有所間則和氣尚鬱而未宣非
樂之達也今焉暴民則不作而孼孽無萌也諸
侯則賓服而靖共不貳也其野有良民而國有
康侯矣乎兵革則不試而武備可弛也五刑則
不用而紀法無奸也其德威惟畏而幾致刑措
矣乎以百姓則無患皡皡然享至治於無虞以
天子則不怒忻忻然樂太平之有象其兆民之
永賴一人之有慶者乎允若茲樂其有不達哉
===
蓋樂雖中出其用則通乎天下而不窮體雖主
靜其效則運於治化而無外樂以平心由天子
以至庶民舉默順於大道之公者非強也惟和
故心平而忻喜懽愛之真機至是其畢達矣乎
樂以宣化由侯服以至王畿舉相安於雍熙之
域者非勉也惟和故化宣而順成和動之妙用
至是其具達矣乎吁此之謂至盛之樂也此之
謂揖讓之治也大樂必易之妙於此可以觀其
深矣雖然樂之達豈一於和者所能哉有為之
punctuated:
者，何以徵之？蓋樂也者，暴戾可化、兵刑可弭、上下可和者也。一有所間，則和氣尚鬱而未宣，非樂之達也。今焉暴民則不作，而孼孽無萌也；諸侯則賓服，而靖共不貳也。其野有良民，而國有康侯矣乎！兵革則不試，而武備可弛也；五刑則不用，而紀法無奸也。其德威惟畏，而幾致刑措矣乎！以百姓則無患，皡皡然享至治於無虞；以天子則不怒，忻忻然樂太平之有象。其兆民之永賴，一人之有慶者乎！允若茲，樂其有不達哉？
蓋樂雖中出，其用則通乎天下而不窮；體雖主靜，其效則運於治化而無外。樂以平心，由天子以至庶民，舉默順於大道之公者，非強也；惟和故心平，而忻喜懽愛之真機，至是其畢達矣乎！樂以宣化，由侯服以至王畿，舉相安於雍熙之域者，非勉也；惟和故化宣，而順成和動之妙用，至是其具達矣乎！吁！此之謂至盛之樂也，此之謂揖讓之治也。「大樂必易」之妙，於此可以觀其深矣。雖然，樂之達豈一於和者所能哉？有為之
translation_en:
… ["When music reaches its perfection, there is no resentment"]—how can this be verified? For music is that by which violent and perverse dispositions can be transformed, weapons and punishments can be laid to rest, and superiors and inferiors can be brought into harmony. If there is the slightest obstruction, then the harmonious vital breath remains pent up and unexpressed; that is not the pervasive reach of music. Now, however, violent people do not arise, and sprouts of evil do not bud; the feudal lords submit in allegiance, quietly and respectfully serving without duplicity. Are there not good people in the countryside and tranquil lords in the states! Arms and armor are not put to use, so military preparations can be relaxed; the Five Punishments are not employed, so none violate the laws and statutes. Is not moral prestige alone held in awe, almost bringing about the setting aside of punishments altogether! As for the common people, they suffer no afflictions, contentedly enjoying consummate governance without anxiety; as for the Son of Heaven, he feels no anger, joyfully delighting in the visible signs of grand peace. Is this not the millions of people eternally relying on the One Man's felicity! Truly being like this, how could music fail to reach everywhere?

For although music issues from within, its function communicates throughout All under Heaven without exhaustion; although its substance is grounded in stillness, its efficacy operates through transformative governance without anything left outside. Music calms the mind: that everyone from the Son of Heaven down to the common people tacitly accords with the impartiality of the Great Way is not due to coercion; only because there is harmony are minds calmed, and has not the true wellspring of joy and loving affection at this point been completely realized! Music proclaims moral transformation: that everyone from the domains of the feudal lords to the royal capital rests at peace together in a realm of harmonious prosperity is not due to forced effort; only because there is harmony is transformation proclaimed, and has not the wondrous function of compliant completion and harmonious movement at this point been fully realized! Ah! This is what is called music at its utmost flourishing; this is what is called governance by courteous deference. The subtlety of the saying "great music is necessarily easy" can herein be observed in its depth. Even so, how could the pervasive reach of music be achieved by harmony alone? There is that which acts as its…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
先者禮是也蓋樂達則情孚禮達則分定苟非
禮以節之而徒曰樂足以化強暴戢兵刑而安
上下也可乎記樂者以樂之達終歸于禮之行
其深於樂者夫
第貳塲
論
正心爲天下萬事之本
周郛
同考試官教諭譚　批　奇崛之才賅博之學精深之思
===
三復令人斂衽
考試官教諭孫　批　格高氣暢一洗塵滓
考試官教授黃　批　雄詞卓識傑士也
善治天下者不以天下爲也握天下之要而已
矣蓋人主者天下所環拱而耳目之者也其窺
我者甚衆所以用其窺我之術者甚密而我心
少有所偏則不待發于音聲形于笑貌而天下
得以識我所向夫惟有以識我所向而緣是以
誘我則必墮其術而不自知是之謂以物爲主
punctuated:
先者，禮是也。蓋樂達則情孚，禮達則分定。苟非禮以節之，而徒曰樂足以化強暴、戢兵刑、而安上下也，可乎？記《樂》者以樂之達終歸于禮之行，其深於樂者夫！

第貳塲

論

正心爲天下萬事之本

周郛

同考試官教諭譚　批：奇崛之才，賅博之學，精深之思，三復令人斂衽。
考試官教諭孫　批：格高氣暢，一洗塵滓。
考試官教授黃　批：雄詞卓識，傑士也。

善治天下者，不以天下爲也，握天下之要而已矣。蓋人主者，天下所環拱而耳目之者也。其窺我者甚衆，所以用其窺我之術者甚密；而我心少有所偏，則不待發于音聲、形于笑貌，而天下得以識我所向。夫惟有以識我所向，而緣是以誘我，則必墮其術而不自知，是之謂以物爲主。
translation_en:
…precedence—and that is ritual. For when music prevails, feelings are brought into mutual trust; when ritual prevails, social distinctions are settled. If there is no ritual to regulate it, and one merely claims that music alone suffices to transform the violent, lay down weapons and punishments, and bring peace to superiors and inferiors—how could that be possible? The writer of the "Record of Music" (Yueji), in attributing the prevailing of music ultimately to the practice of ritual, was truly one who understood music deeply!

Second Session

Discourse

"Rectifying the Mind Is the Fundamental Basis of the Myriad Affairs of the World"

Zhou Fu 周郛

Associate Examiner, County Director of Studies Tan 譚 comments: "Extraordinary and towering talent, comprehensive learning, and refined, profound thought—reading it three times makes one adjust one's lapels in respect."
Examiner, County Director of Studies Sun 孫 comments: "Lofty in style and fluent in vital energy, washing away all worldly dross."
Examiner, Prefectural Director of Studies Huang 黃 comments: "Vigorous diction and outstanding insight—an exceptional scholar."

Those who are skilled at governing the world do not busy themselves with the world itself; they simply grasp the essential pivot of the world, and that is all. For the ruler of men is the one whom the whole world surrounds and watches and listens to. Those who spy upon me are very numerous, and the arts they employ to spy upon me are exceedingly subtle. If my mind has the slightest partiality, then without waiting for it to be uttered in voice or tone, or manifested in smile or countenance, the world is already able to discern my inclinations. Now once they have the means to discern my inclinations and use them to entice me, I will inevitably fall into their schemes without realizing it. This is what is meant by letting external things be the master.…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
惟正吾之心則我能先天下以用其察而天下
無所用其窺是之謂以我爲主物爲主則汨沒
于萬物之中而何以理物我爲主則超然于萬
物之上而物自可正此所謂握天下之要也善
哉朱氏之言正心爲天下萬事之本也蓋世主
之治天下有粥粥焉役耳目以當轇轕之衝矣
而不知耳目之用爲用也末十里之間而耳不
塞九有若之何哉惟心者徹乎天地通乎神明
===
洞乎晻昧貫乎遠近先後千變萬化無不本焉
固道之窾係而治之樞紐也然而出入無常動
靜靡測著者或微安者或危未易正也而在人
主爲尤難蓋天下之物可喜可玩而足以動人
者日紛紛于前而天下之人求進其喜玩以使
吾之悅慕不舍者日相逐于左右不特冶容珍
味藻繡彫甍爲然而凡所以移易吾意者莫不
未形而爲之啓當先而爲之逢旣事而爲之遂
已謬而爲之文而吾不能正其心以待之則邪
punctuated: 惟正吾之心，則我能先天下以用其察，而天下無所用其窺，是之謂以我爲主。物爲主，則汨沒于萬物之中，而何以理物？我爲主，則超然于萬物之上，而物自可正。此所謂握天下之要也。善哉朱氏之言，「正心爲天下萬事之本」也！蓋世主之治天下，有粥粥焉役耳目以當轇轕之衝矣，而不知耳目之用爲用也末。十里之間而耳不塞，九有若之何哉？惟心者，徹乎天地，通乎神明，洞乎晻昧，貫乎遠近先後，千變萬化無不本焉，固道之窾係而治之樞紐也。然而出入無常，動靜靡測，著者或微，安者或危，未易正也，而在人主爲尤難。蓋天下之物，可喜可玩而足以動人者，日紛紛于前；而天下之人，求進其喜玩以使吾之悅慕不舍者，日相逐于左右。不特冶容珍味、藻繡彫甍爲然，而凡所以移易吾意者，莫不未形而爲之啓，當先而爲之逢，旣事而爲之遂，已謬而爲之文。而吾不能正其心以待之，則邪
translation_en: … Whereas if I rectify my mind, I can exercise my discernment ahead of the world, and the world will have no way to employ its spying. This is what is meant by taking the self as master. When external things are master, one sinks and drowns amid the myriad things—so how could one bring order to things? When the self is master, one stands transcendent above the myriad things, and things can naturally be set right. This is what is called grasping the essential pivot of the realm. How excellent are the words of Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹], that "rectifying the mind is the foundation of the myriad affairs of the world"! Indeed, when rulers of the world govern the realm, some anxiously enslaving their ears and eyes to confront the onslaught of tangled complexities, yet fail to realize that the function of the ears and eyes is a minor one. Even within a distance of ten li, the ears cannot take everything in [?]; what then of the Nine Regions of the empire? Only the mind penetrates heaven and earth, communicates with the spirits and gods, sees through obscurity and darkness, and threads together the far and near, the prior and subsequent; the myriad transformations and changes are all rooted therein. Truly it is the crucial nexus of the Way and the central hinge of governance. Yet its going out and coming in are inconstant, its movement and stillness unfathomable; what is manifest may become subtle, and what is secure may become perilous. It is not easy to rectify, and for the ruler of men it is especially difficult. For the things of the world that are delightful and amusing and sufficient to stir a person appear in profusion before him every day; and the people of the world who seek to present such delights and amusements so as to make him infatuated and unable to let go chase after one another at his side every day. This is true not only of seductive looks and rare delicacies, ornate embroideries and carved roof-beams; in everything that might shift and alter his intentions, there is none who does not open the way for it before it has even taken shape, anticipate and cater to it beforehand, carry it through once the matter is underway, and gloss over it once an error has been made. And if I cannot rectify my mind in order to meet them, then evil…

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
壬之伏其中於心也微而其植根也膠而難解
苟一不解則微者或横潰而著矣根者或引蔓
而枝矣至于潰且蔓則雖有賢人君子以維持
而匡弼之靡益矣故夫心之不可以不正而正
之爲未易也夫冶容珍味藻繡彫甍猶其末也
是數者可以誘中主而不可以誘聰明之主惟
天下之攻于誘者雖聰明之主而有所不能逃
其術至于不能逃其術則雖不正而不自知也
是故心向于治若正也而或申韓之偏見藉以
入也心向于學若正也而或公孫安石之曲學
藉以入也心向于文若正也而或徐庾之淫艶
藉以入也心志于事業若正也而或桑孔之財
利衞霍之武功藉以入也何也彼數者之欲售
其術而恐莫售也必張虛美飾小效以薫吾心
而快吾意俾吾眩于其美而惑于其效自以爲
治平無事也于是廣侈其志厭縱其欲而冶容
珍味藻繡彫甍之類亦且浸淫而至至于横潰
而不自覺不知天下之實禍隱憂于兹醞釀矣
punctuated: 壬之伏，其中於心也微，而其植根也膠而難解。苟一不解，則微者或横潰而著矣，根者或引蔓而枝矣。至于潰且蔓，則雖有賢人君子以維持而匡弼之，靡益矣。故夫心之不可以不正，而正之爲未易也。夫冶容、珍味、藻繡、彫甍，猶其末也，是數者可以誘中主，而不可以誘聰明之主。惟天下之攻于誘者，雖聰明之主，而有所不能逃其術；至于不能逃其術，則雖不正而不自知也。是故心向于治，若正也，而或申、韓之偏見藉以入也；心向于學，若正也，而或公孫、安石之曲學藉以入也；心向于文，若正也，而或徐、庾之淫艶藉以入也；心志于事業，若正也，而或桑、孔之財利，衞、霍之武功藉以入也。何也？彼數者之欲售其術而恐莫售也，必張虛美、飾小效以薫吾心而快吾意，俾吾眩于其美而惑于其效，自以爲治平無事也。于是廣侈其志，厭縱其欲，而冶容、珍味、藻繡、彫甍之類，亦且浸淫而至，至于横潰而不自覺，不知天下之實禍隱憂于兹醞釀矣。
translation_en:
…and sycophantic men will lie in wait: their striking at the mind is subtle, and their taking root is fast and hard to untangle. Should it once go unloosened, what was subtle may burst forth wildly and become manifest, and what had taken root may send out creepers and branch out. When it reaches the point of bursting forth and spreading, then even if there are worthy men and gentlemen to sustain and rectify him, it will be of no avail. Therefore, the mind cannot but be rectified, and yet to rectify it is no easy matter.

Now alluring countenances, rare delicacies, fine embroideries, and carved roof-beams are still merely the superficialities; these several things can seduce a mediocre ruler, but cannot seduce an intelligent and discerning ruler. Only against those in the world who specialize in seduction can even an intelligent and discerning ruler in some respects fail to escape their arts; and when it comes to not being able to escape their arts, then even when his mind is not rectified, he himself does not realize it.

Therefore, when his mind is inclined toward governance, it seems rectified, yet perhaps the biased views of Shen Buhai (申不害) and Han Fei (韓非) avail themselves of this to enter; when his mind is inclined toward learning, it seems rectified, yet perhaps the crooked learning of Gongsun Hong (公孫弘) and Wang Anshi (王安石) avails itself of this to enter; when his mind is inclined toward literature, it seems rectified, yet perhaps the licentious floridity of Xu Ling (徐陵) and Yu Xin (庾信) avails itself of this to enter; when his mind is set upon great enterprises, it seems rectified, yet perhaps the financial profiteering of Sang Hongyang (桑弘羊) and Kong Jin (孔僅) or the military exploits of Wei Qing (衞青) and Huo Qubing (霍去病) avail themselves of this to enter. Why is this? Because when those several sorts of men wish to peddle their arts and fear they will not be accepted, they inevitably exaggerate empty beauties and dress up petty results to Steep our mind and gratify our intentions, causing us to be dazzled by their beauties and deluded by their results, supposing ourselves that the realm is well-governed, peaceful, and free of trouble. Thereupon, as he broadens and indulges his ambitions and sates his desires without restraint, things of the sort of alluring countenances, rare delicacies, fine embroideries, and carved roof-beams will also gradually seep in and arrive, until it reaches a wild bursting-forth without his realizing it himself, not knowing that the real disasters and hidden sorrows of the empire are being brewed right here.

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
其始也欲爲上主之所爲而其繼也乃爲中主
之所不爲雖粥粥于耳目不過帷幄之間十里
之内自爲治耳天下萬事孰得其當哉蓋能正
其心則吾之聰明爲我之用而權自我握不正
其心則吾之聰明適爲邪壬之資而權不屬于
我矣聖主知其然也不求正于天下而求正于
心精之一之克之復之無日而不珍攝無日而
不完養不使有一毫之妄念邪動以累我虛靈
之天幽獨燕閑之中而若對上帝若趨宗廟女
===
謁近習之前而若見法家弼士父兄師保紛華
波蕩可以馳逞之際而若百官六軍萬姓之列
于傍而議我也無晝夜無久暫如養珠如抱卵
如棒盂水而方寸之地不爲五官百骸所勝矣
然猶懼其或陷于過失而不自知也委任輔弼
廣開耳目而凡其一職一事苟有關于國家之
理亂而係于人主之心術者莫不統于冢宰焉
虎賁綴衣不以爲細人也飲膳烹庖酒漿醯醢
不以爲微物也掃灑縫染不以爲賤職也幄帟
punctuated: 其始也，欲爲上主之所爲；而其繼也，乃爲中主之所不爲。雖粥粥于耳目，不過帷幄之間、十里之内自爲治耳，天下萬事孰得其當哉？蓋能正其心，則吾之聰明爲我之用，而權自我握；不正其心，則吾之聰明適爲邪壬之資，而權不屬于我矣。聖主知其然也，不求正于天下而求正于心，精之、一之、克之、復之，無日而不珍攝，無日而不完養，不使有一毫之妄念邪動以累我虛靈之天。幽獨燕閑之中，而若對上帝，若趨宗廟；女謁近習之前，而若見法家弼士、父兄師保；紛華波蕩、可以馳逞之際，而若百官、六軍、萬姓之列于傍而議我也。無晝夜，無久暫，如養珠，如抱卵，如棒盂水，而方寸之地不爲五官百骸所勝矣。然猶懼其或陷于過失而不自知也，委任輔弼，廣開耳目，而凡其一職一事，苟有關于國家之理亂而係于人主之心術者，莫不統于冢宰焉。虎賁、綴衣，不以爲細人也；飲膳、烹庖、酒漿、醯醢，不以爲微物也；掃灑、縫染，不以爲賤職也；幄帟、
translation_en: At the outset, one wishes to do what the highest rulers did, yet subsequently ends up doing what even mediocre rulers would not do. Even if one appears cautiously diligent before people's eyes and ears, this is merely creating a semblance of order within the curtains of the palace or inside a radius of ten li; among the myriad affairs of the empire, which of them will be handled properly? For if one can rectify the mind, then one's intelligence and perception are at one's own disposal, and authority is grasped in one's own hands; if one does not rectify the mind, then one's intelligence and perception merely serve as capital for wicked flatterers, and authority no longer belongs to oneself. The sage ruler knows that this is so. He does not seek rectification in the empire, but seeks rectification in his own mind—refining it, unifying it, mastering himself, and returning to propriety. There is no day that he does not cherish and guard it, no day that he does not nurture and complete it, never allowing the slightest deluded thought or perverse impulse to encumber the pure spiritual nature of his heaven-endowed mind. In the solitude of private leisure, it is as though he were facing the Lord on High, or hastening into the ancestral temple; before female petitioners and intimate attendants, it is as though he were seeing law-abiding ministers, upright counselors, elder kinsmen, and Grand Preceptors and Grand Guardians; at moments of dazzling luxury and surging temptation when he might give free rein to his desires, it is as though the hundred officials, the six armies, and the myriad common people were lined up beside him passing judgment on him. Whether day or night, whether for a long time or a brief moment, it is like nurturing a pearl, like brooding over eggs, or like holding up a bowl of water [reading 棒 as 捧], so that the square inch of his mind is not overcome by the five senses and the hundred bodily parts. Yet, still fearing that he might fall into error without realizing it himself, he entrusts responsibility to his輔弼 (coadjutors and assistants) and broadly opens his ears and eyes. Every single office and every single affair, so long as it has bearing on the order or disorder of the state and is connected to the dispositions of the ruler's mind, is without exception placed under the general control of the Minister of State (zhongzai). The Warrior Guards (huben) and keepers of the robes (zhuiyi) are not regarded as trivial personnel; food and drink, cooking and kitchen work, wines, beverages, vinegar, and meat sauces are not regarded as petty matters; sweeping, sprinkling, sewing, and dyeing are not regarded as lowly offices; curtains, canopies, …

title: 萬曆十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
次舍不以爲小事也要皆制以有司之法而俾
吾之舉動有所礙而不敢自恣紀綱不散名分
不易爵祿不輕而左右前後無敢有蠱吾之心
術以浸淫于政事如是則天理盎然充滿具足
無欲無惡無偏無黨兼陳萬象懸衡其中而天
下之聽唱而應視儀而動者孰敢不正縱有險
壬之伏不待察而若望參表矣是故申韓不能
惑而天下靡慘刻之害也公孫安石不能迷而
天下靡紛更之害也徐庾不能蕩而天下靡淫
麗之患也桑孔不能謀而天下免椎剝之患也
衛霍不能奮而天下免骨白燐青之患也由是
修制則禮樂昭明由是稽績則品式周備由是
布澤則湛恩龐鴻由是詳刑則獄訟清簡羣辟
摶心揖志以象其指庶吽矯手頓足以詠其澤
而天子者惟端委恭已而已不出闈閾不離表
著而經緯乾坤衡鏡宇宙外運渾元内霈毫芒
以至黃支之南大夏之西東鞮北女此心無所
不達而莫敢有矯命而雄行睨視而跂望者豈
punctuated: 次舍，不以爲小事也。要皆制以有司之法，而俾吾之舉動有所礙而不敢自恣，紀綱不散，名分不易，爵祿不輕，而左右前後無敢有蠱吾之心術以浸淫于政事。如是則天理盎然，充滿具足，無欲無惡，無偏無黨，兼陳萬象，懸衡其中，而天下之聽唱而應、視儀而動者，孰敢不正？縱有險壬之伏，不待察而若望參表矣。是故申、韓不能惑，而天下靡慘刻之害也；公孫、安石不能迷，而天下靡紛更之害也；徐、庾不能蕩，而天下靡淫麗之患也；桑、孔不能謀，而天下免椎剝之患也；衛、霍不能奮，而天下免骨白燐青之患也。由是修制，則禮樂昭明；由是稽績，則品式周備；由是布澤，則湛恩龐鴻；由是詳刑，則獄訟清簡。羣辟摶心揖志，以象其指；庶吽矯手頓足，以詠其澤。而天子者，惟端委恭已而已。不出闈閾，不離表著，而經緯乾坤，衡鏡宇宙，外運渾元，内霈毫芒，以至黃支之南、大夏之西、東鞮、北女，此心無所不達，而莫敢有矯命而雄行、睨視而跂望者。豈
translation_en: … and tented lodgings are not regarded as trivial affairs. In sum, all are regulated by the statutes of the authorities, so that my every movement encounters restraint and I dare not indulge myself; the fundamental order does not slacken, status and duty are not altered, ranks and emoluments are not treated lightly, and among my attendants on all sides none dares beguile the workings of my mind so as to seep into the affairs of governance. When it is thus, Heavenly Principle brims forth, full and complete: without selfish desire or aversion, without partiality or faction, arraying all phenomena together and suspending the balance in their midst. Among all in the empire who hear the call and respond, who look upon the model and act, who would dare not be upright? Even if treacherous and artful men should lurk in hiding, without waiting for investigation they will be as plain as gazing at a gnomon.
